claim: What a passing run establishes is bounded, and the bound differs between the two kinds of observation this campaign takes. For the exact-count resources — framework-owned tasks, pooled connections, connection checkouts, and process handles — the claim is non-accumulation: they are integers and every measured cycle boundary held them at the post-warmup baseline. For resident memory the claim is weaker and is stated as what the rule actually decides: resident-memory growth converged under the declared rate-decay rule. That rule does not exclude a sufficiently small leak masked by settling behaviour, so no exact non-accumulation claim is made about RSS. Both claims hold only over the declared warmup and measured window, running the declared workload against a supported PostgreSQL, and every cycle's durable record equalled the first measured cycle's. It is not a claim that no leak exists over an unbounded period, and it is not a budget. A resource that is not observed here is unexamined rather than proved absent.
notes: The report is run on its own so its result is attributable, and the fixture is resolved before it starts, because a soak that skipped for want of a database returns success.

A passing report is not sufficient, and a soak has a failure mode the other campaigns do not. Every other campaign's obligation exists independently of its run — a ledger row, a commit phase, a schema path, a declared ceiling — so a report either covered it or did not. A soak's obligation is a period, and a soak that ran three cycles and one that ran three hundred produce reports of identical shape. The shorter one produces the flatter series and therefore the more convincing result. So this runner reads the committed denominator and requires the declared warmup and measured windows to have run, with a sample per cycle.

It also requires the workload to be the declared one, down to the partition count, worker budget, and pool size, and requires the lifecycle to have happened once per cycle: a fault injected, a restart, a recovery, and a completed drain. A run that repeated a plain launch would otherwise satisfy every window requirement and produce the same flat series.

Every declared correctness obligation must have been decided and must hold before any resource number counts, because resource flatness over a workload that stopped doing the work is not a result. Every declared growth rule must have been decided, must have applied the rule the campaign declares, must carry the series it was decided from, and must have passed.

What a passing run establishes is bounded by the declared window and the declared workload. It is not a claim that no leak exists over an unbounded period, and the durable history the database accumulates on purpose is recorded beside the process series rather than counted as growth.

The report is required to name the PostgreSQL major it ran against, because a matrix point is invisible in a connection string and an observation from one supported major would otherwise reconcile perfectly inside a run of another.

out_of_scope.why: The cancellation campaign is a separate row of the accepted plan with its own latency reports. This campaign drains at every cycle boundary and requires the drain to complete, which is not the same obligation as measuring request-to-intake-stop and request-to-durable-terminal latency.

Separate campaign rows. Nothing here is compared against a time budget, and the cycle duration is recorded as context rather than asserted on, so a loaded host makes this campaign slower rather than red.
A separate campaign row. This workload is a lifecycle exerciser sized to make resource accumulation visible, not a representative deployment.
The claim is about the declared window. A longer window is a different campaign result, not a stronger reading of this one.

related.invariant: 24 in-memory cycles of launch, failure, restart, and drain, with the same durable observation and the same repository work each cycle
related.name: p015_shutdown_restart_soak
related.note: The M4 measurement this campaign builds on and does not replace. It is the baseline: it fixed the per-cycle semantics — every owned task joined, the same repository work, the same durable observation, no re-run of a committed partition — and this campaign keeps them. What it cannot supply is M5 evidence, because it builds a fresh in-memory repository every cycle. That resets the two observations a production-preview soak is mostly about, connections and handles, and it means the resident reading it takes is over a process holding no pool. Its result is retained as an M4 measurement and is not cited as a PostgreSQL result.

related.invariant: peak partition-worker occupancy equals the configured budget and a pool one connection short is refused before any child starts
related.name: declared_ceilings_hold_under_stress_with_backpressure
related.note: The resource-bound campaign proves a ceiling holds under a single stressed run. This campaign asks a different question of the same resources: whether the level they return to is the level they started at, over many runs. A ceiling that holds every time and a baseline that rises every time are both possible at once.
